title: A Resort on Tsuut’ina Nation Land
body:
Grey Eagle Resort & Casino is located on the lands of the Tsuut’ina Nation, just outside Calgary. The resort is proudly owned and operated by the Nation and brings together contemporary hospitality, entertainment, dining, and Indigenous heritage. This connection to place is an important part of the Grey Eagle experience: visitors are not simply arriving at a resort, but entering a destination shaped by the people, history, and living culture of the Tsuut’ina Nation.
That cultural connection can be explored through guided experiences, storytelling, Indigenous-inspired dining, and opportunities to learn more about the Nation’s relationship with its land and community. Grey Eagle presents culture as part of the wider visitor experience rather than as something separate from the destination itself.

title: The Meaning of Tsuut’ina
body:
According to Tsuut’ina Elders, the name Tsuut’ina can be understood as either “many people” or “beaver people,” and both interpretations are recognized by the Nation. The name represents a distinct Indigenous identity with its own language, cultural traditions, history, and relationship to the land.
The Tsuut’ina are connected linguistically and culturally to the wider Dene peoples and are the only Dene-speaking Nation within Treaty 7 Territory. Today, maintaining this distinct identity remains closely connected with language, cultural knowledge, self-determination, and the continued transmission of traditions between generations.

title: Language as Living Heritage
body:
The Tsuut’ina language, Tsúūt’ínà Gūnáhà, belongs to the Dene language family and is one of the most distinctive parts of the Nation’s cultural identity. Language carries more than vocabulary: it connects generations, preserves ways of describing the world, and helps maintain stories, values, names, and cultural knowledge.
The Nation continues language revitalization efforts through recording, teaching, written resources, and pronunciation materials. Even common expressions such as greetings and words of thanks become a way for new generations to reconnect with a language that carries the memory and identity of their people. The Tsuut’ina Gunaha Institute plays an important role in supporting this continuing work.

title: The Tsuut’ina Museum Experience
body:
One of the cultural experiences offered through Grey Eagle begins with a guided introduction at the Tsuut’ina Museum. Rather than presenting culture only through objects, the experience introduces visitors to Tsuut’ina history, storytelling, language, and traditions through knowledgeable cultural guides.
The tour is designed as an introduction to a living culture. Visitors are encouraged to understand that heritage continues through the people who preserve language, share stories, maintain community knowledge, and interpret history from a Tsuut’ina perspective. It provides an opportunity to learn directly within the cultural context of the Nation rather than treating its history as something belonging only to the past.

title: Buffalo, Land & Cultural Connection
body:
The buffalo holds deep cultural and historical significance, and Grey Eagle’s Buffalo Paddock Tour gives visitors an opportunity to encounter that connection through a guided outdoor experience. The tour includes interpretation of the buffalo herd and explores the relationship between buffalo, land, and tradition.
The experience is not presented simply as wildlife viewing. Instead, the buffalo becomes an entry point for understanding the broader relationship between Indigenous peoples and the landscapes that supported their communities across generations. The tour connects the physical environment with cultural memory and provides visitors with a more meaningful perspective on the land surrounding the Nation.

title: Indigenous Culture in Motion
body:
The DH Ranch Indigenous Experience introduces visitors to Indian Relay and ranch life through a setting where culture, horses, skill, and teamwork come together. Guests can learn about the relay tradition, interact with horses, see demonstrations, and meet members of the DH Ranch relay team.
Indian Relay requires trust between rider and horse, precise timing, physical ability, and close cooperation among team members. Through this experience, visitors can see a contemporary expression of Indigenous identity that connects cultural continuity with modern competition, horsemanship, and community life.

title: Learning Through Storytelling
body:
Grey Eagle’s cultural experiences place storytelling at the centre of cultural learning. The Brown Bear Woman Events Cultural Experience includes Indigenous teachings, interpretive activities, educational programming, storytelling, and cultural awareness sessions.
Storytelling allows history and knowledge to be approached through voices and perspectives that are connected to the community itself. Rather than reducing culture to a list of dates or objects, these experiences encourage visitors to understand how knowledge can be shared through stories, teachings, relationships, and lived experience.

title: Indigenous-Inspired Dining
body:
Food can also become part of the cultural experience at Grey Eagle. Cultural tour groups may add dining to their visit, including the option of an Indigenous-inspired meal at Little Chief Restaurant. Grey Eagle identifies Indigenous influence as one of the distinctive elements within its culinary offerings.
Including dining alongside cultural tours allows visitors to experience the destination through more than one form of interpretation. Stories, land, hospitality, and food can become interconnected parts of the visit, creating a broader understanding of how contemporary Indigenous identity can be expressed within a modern resort environment.

title: The Story of Separation
body:
One of the publicly shared Tsuut’ina migration stories tells of a time when the ancestors of the Tsuut’ina were travelling south in search of food. The people reached a frozen lake, and their Chiefs instructed everyone to cross quickly because the ice was thin.
During the crossing, a child noticed an object protruding from the ice and began crying for it. His mother eventually tried to cut the object free. According to the story, what appeared to be an object was actually the horn of Tāstłāní, a dragon. The creature moved, the ice broke, and the people became separated. Some remained or travelled north while the Tsuut’ina continued south.
The Nation describes this as one account of the separation of the Tsuut’ina from the Northern Dene. It has been passed through generations, while the Tsuut’ina Nation also emphasizes that oral-history accounts may vary between families and that these different perspectives are respected.

title: The Journey South
body:
Migration is an important part of the publicly shared history of the Tsuut’ina people. The Nation’s historical narrative describes ancestors travelling through northern Alberta and gradually moving south while searching for food and places that could sustain their communities.
The migration story is closely connected with the wider Dene world and helps explain the historical relationship between the Tsuut’ina and other Dene peoples. Today, the Tsuut’ina Nation is located southwest of Calgary, but stories of movement and separation remain an important part of understanding where the people came from and how their distinct identity developed over generations.

title: Everything Is Connected
body:
The Tsuut’ina Nation describes a worldview in which life is interconnected and sacred. Human beings are understood as one part of a much larger circle that includes the land and the elements of water, air, and fire. This relationship forms part of what the Nation describes as Natural Law.
From this perspective, land is more than a physical setting. It is part of a network of relationships that carries responsibility, meaning, and continuity. Respect for these relationships helps explain why land, animals, language, community, and cultural teachings cannot always be separated into individual subjects: together, they form part of a wider way of understanding the world.

title: The Beaver Bundle
body:
Within the Tsuut’ina separation story, the Beaver Bundle appears as part of the Nation’s memory of migration. The publicly shared account explains that during the people’s travels, the Beaver Bundle moved ahead with the camp using a dog travois.
The story connects the Bundle with the journey of the ancestors and with cultural continuity across generations. The official Tsuut’ina account explains that this historical connection is part of why the Beaver Bundle remains with the people today.

title: Treaty No. 7
body:
In 1877, Head Chief Chiila Bullhead entered Treaty No. 7 with the British Crown on behalf of the Tsuut’ina Nation. The Nation presents Treaty 7 as part of its continuing political and historical identity and emphasizes that Tsuut’ina sovereignty, inherent rights, Treaty rights, and responsibilities remain fundamental to the Nation’s understanding of itself.
For visitors, Treaty 7 is therefore more than a date in a historical timeline. It remains connected with questions of land, governance, relationships, responsibility, and self-determination. Understanding this context helps place the modern Tsuut’ina Nation and its economic, cultural, and community initiatives within a much longer history.

title: Tsuut’ina Day
body:
The Tsuut’ina Nation’s official historical timeline records May 1 as Tsuut’ina Day, a holiday for the people. The date was selected because this period traditionally marked the beginning of another life cycle following winter.
The Nation explains that this time was associated with giving thanks to the Great Spirit, making important decisions, and gathering for feasts and dances. In this way, the day connects seasonal change with community life and collective renewal. It is an example of how cultural traditions can connect time, land, community, and celebration within a shared annual rhythm.

title: Stories Passed Through Generations
body:
Oral history remains important because a story can carry knowledge that is difficult to express through dates alone. Stories may preserve memories of migration, relationships with the land, family knowledge, cultural values, and explanations of how communities understand their own past.
The Tsuut’ina Nation explicitly notes that oral histories can vary from one family to another. Rather than treating these differences as errors, the Nation acknowledges and respects multiple perspectives. This is an important principle when learning about Indigenous history: cultural stories belong to living communities, and different families may preserve different versions or details while continuing to share a broader cultural memory.

title: Heritage in the Present Day
body:
Tsuut’ina heritage is not limited to historical events. The Nation describes itself today through language, traditional protocols, leadership, artists, athletes, students, cowboys, visionaries, and modern-day warriors. Culture continues through everyday community life as well as through formal cultural programs.
Grey Eagle reflects part of this contemporary story. As a Tsuut’ina-owned and operated destination, it combines economic development, hospitality, cultural experiences, tourism, and support for Indigenous businesses and artists. The result is an example of heritage continuing alongside modern Nationhood rather than existing only as a memory of the past.

title: Culture Designed to Be Experienced
body:
Grey Eagle’s cultural program is built around direct experiences rather than passive observation. Its Cultural Tours invite visitors to explore Tsuut’ina culture, history, and connection to the land through guided activities that can combine museum interpretation, storytelling, language, buffalo, horses, traditional teachings, and Indigenous-inspired dining.
The tours are designed primarily for groups of approximately 10–14 people, although experiences can be customized depending on group size and interests. This flexible format allows each visit to focus on the aspects of Tsuut’ina culture that are most meaningful for a particular group while still being guided by knowledgeable cultural representatives.

title: Knowledge Shared by Cultural Guides
body:
A key part of the Grey Eagle cultural experience is the opportunity to learn through knowledgeable cultural guides. During the guided experience connected with the Tsuut’ina Museum, visitors are introduced to history, storytelling, language, and traditions within a structured cultural setting.
This approach gives the experience an important human dimension. Instead of encountering heritage only through written descriptions, guests can learn through interpretation and storytelling connected directly to the community. The guide becomes a bridge between the visitor and the cultural context of what they are seeing, helping make the experience more thoughtful and meaningful.

title: Culture, History & Land Together
body:
Grey Eagle describes its cultural tours as an opportunity to experience the culture, history, and land of the Tsuut’ina Nation. These three elements are intentionally presented together because the cultural story of the Nation cannot be understood only through historic dates or museum objects.
The Buffalo Paddock Tour makes this relationship especially visible. Visitors encounter the buffalo herd in an outdoor setting while learning about the animal’s cultural and historical significance and its connection to land and tradition. The landscape therefore becomes part of the learning experience itself, connecting cultural interpretation with the physical place where the Nation continues to live today.

title: Indian Relay — Culture in Motion
body:
The DH Ranch Indigenous Experience introduces visitors to Indian Relay and ranch life through an active and contemporary cultural experience. Rather than presenting Indigenous culture only through historical displays, the program allows guests to see horses, relay demonstrations, and members of the DH Ranch relay team.
The experience emphasizes three important elements: trust, timing, and teamwork. Riders and team members must coordinate closely while working with horses, making Indian Relay a powerful example of skill, cooperation, and living cultural expression. Visitors can see how horsemanship remains part of contemporary Indigenous life while learning directly from people involved in the tradition today.

title: Learning Through Participation
body:
The Brown Bear Woman Events Cultural Experience is designed around active cultural learning. Grey Eagle describes the program as including interactive educational programming, traditional teachings, interpretive experiences, Indigenous storytelling, and cultural awareness sessions.
This format moves beyond simply reading information about Indigenous culture. Visitors are encouraged to engage with teachings and stories through a guided experience where explanation, participation, and interpretation work together. The purpose is not only to present cultural information, but to create an environment where guests can better understand the meaning and context behind what they are learning.

title: A Cultural Experience Shaped for Each Group
body:
Grey Eagle does not present its cultural tours as a fixed, identical itinerary for every visitor. The program is offered by request and can be customized depending on the size and interests of the group.
Groups may focus more heavily on museum learning, the buffalo experience, Indigenous teachings, Indian Relay, or combine multiple activities into a broader visit. Optional dining can also be added. This approach allows the cultural program to remain flexible while creating an experience that is more relevant to the people taking part.
Because availability depends on cultural guides and tour scheduling, each experience is arranged individually rather than functioning like a standard walk-in attraction.

title: Contemporary Indigenous Creativity
body:
Tsuut’ina cultural identity continues to appear in contemporary art, media, sport, and design. The Nation’s official historical timeline records milestones that demonstrate how cultural expression continues to evolve rather than remaining tied exclusively to the past.
One recent example is Tsuut’ina Nation Citizen Keegan Starlight, who designed the 2026 Calgary Flames Indigenous Celebration logo and jersey artwork. The Nation also highlights the creation of the Oki Corral Film Festival, organized by Tsuut’ina Nation Citizen Kevin Littlelight to celebrate Tsuut’ina and Treaty 7 filmmakers and writers.
These examples show heritage being expressed through modern visual design, storytelling, film, and public events while remaining connected to Indigenous identity.

title: Nationhood in a Modern Setting
body:
The Tsuut’ina Nation describes itself as a sovereign people whose identity continues through language, customs, traditions, territory, governance, and community life. At the same time, the Nation has developed major contemporary economic and community initiatives.
Grey Eagle is part of that modern story. Rather than separating Indigenous identity from contemporary development, the destination demonstrates how hospitality, tourism, entertainment, dining, and cultural experiences can exist alongside cultural continuity and Nationhood.
For visitors, this provides an important perspective: Indigenous heritage is not simply something to look back on. It continues through decisions, enterprises, cultural programs, artists, leaders, families, and community institutions operating today.

title: Chief Bullhead and the Protection of the Land
body:
Chief Bullhead occupies an important place in Tsuut’ina history. The Nation’s official historical timeline records periods when pressure was placed on the community to surrender parts of its reserve. Chief Bullhead and other leaders resisted these efforts and maintained that the land should remain for the people.
This history demonstrates the importance of land not simply as property, but as a foundation for community continuity, identity, governance, and future generations. The Nation’s historical account preserves Chief Bullhead’s determination to resist further loss of reserve land during a period when Indigenous communities across Canada were facing extensive outside pressure.
His leadership remains part of the wider story of Tsuut’ina resilience and the continuing relationship between people, territory, and self-determination.

title: Treaty 7 as a Continuing Relationship
body:
Treaty 7 is a central part of Tsuut’ina political and historical identity. Head Chief Chiila Bullhead entered Treaty 7 with representatives of the British Crown in 1877 alongside other First Nations of southern Alberta.
From the Tsuut’ina perspective presented by the Nation today, Treaty is not simply a document belonging to the nineteenth century. The Nation continues to emphasize its inherent rights, Treaty rights, responsibilities, and self-determination.
This makes Treaty 7 part of a living relationship rather than only a historical milestone. Understanding that distinction is important when learning about the modern Nation, because questions of land, governance, rights, and responsibility continue to influence Tsuut’ina life in the present.

title: Why Oral Histories May Be Different
body:
Tsuut’ina history has been carried through generations not only in written records, but also through oral traditions. Different families may preserve different details or versions of the same historical event or cultural story.
The Nation acknowledges these differences rather than treating a single version as the only acceptable account. This is especially important when encountering stories about migration, separation, important leaders, or the movement of the people.
Oral history is therefore not simply an alternative form of a textbook. It is a living way of preserving knowledge through families and generations. Listening respectfully to different accounts helps preserve the diversity of perspectives within the community rather than forcing them into one standardized narrative.

title: A Nation Connected to the Dene
body:
The Tsuut’ina Nation identifies a strong connection with the wider Dene world through language, culture, customs, and historical territory. The Nation is particularly distinctive because it is the only Dene-speaking Nation within Treaty 7 Territory.
This connection helps explain why Tsuut’ina identity contains relationships that extend both northward toward other Dene peoples and locally within the Treaty 7 region of southern Alberta.
Stories of migration and separation preserve part of this history. Although the Tsuut’ina eventually developed their own distinct territory and political relationships in the south, linguistic and cultural connections continue to provide an important link to their Dene origins.

title: The Sacred Circle
body:
The Tsuut’ina Nation describes a worldview in which people exist as only one part of a larger sacred circle. Water, air, fire, land, people, and other elements of the natural world are interconnected rather than existing independently.
The Nation associates these relationships with Natural Law and emphasizes that inherent Tsuut’ina values should be respected in decisions made today. This way of thinking places responsibility alongside belonging: being connected to the land also means recognizing duties toward the relationships that sustain life.
For visitors learning about Tsuut’ina culture, this concept provides useful context for understanding why discussions of land, buffalo, community, language, history, and identity frequently overlap rather than appearing as completely separate subjects.

title: From Winter to a New Life Cycle
body:
The origins of Tsuut’ina Day, celebrated on May 1, are connected with seasonal change and renewal. According to the Nation’s historical timeline, this period traditionally followed the end of winter and marked the beginning of another life cycle.
It was a time when people gathered, gave thanks to the Great Spirit, made important decisions, and celebrated through feasts and dances. Historical Tsuut’ina materials also describe the period as an opportunity for the community to come together after winter and observe changes within the population.
The tradition therefore connects the natural cycle of the seasons with renewal, community gathering, gratitude, decision-making, and collective identity.

title: Language Carries More Than Words
body:
For the Tsuut’ina Nation, language is one of the defining elements of cultural identity. Tsúūt’ínà Gūnáhà connects the Nation with its Dene linguistic heritage while also distinguishing the Tsuut’ina within Treaty 7 Territory.
Language carries ways of naming people, places, relationships, cultural concepts, and experiences that may not always translate precisely into English. It also connects generations because spoken words can carry cultural knowledge alongside their literal meaning.
The continued use and teaching of the language therefore represents more than preservation of vocabulary. It is part of maintaining a distinct Tsuut’ina identity and ensuring that cultural knowledge can continue to move from one generation to the next.

title: Culture Is Still Being Written
body:
The history of the Tsuut’ina Nation does not end with Treaty 7 or with stories from earlier generations. The Nation’s official timeline continues into the present and includes contemporary developments in housing, commerce, filmmaking, art, sport, and cultural representation.
This is an important way to understand heritage: every generation contributes something to the continuing story. Traditional knowledge and historical memory remain important, but new achievements also become part of the Nation’s cultural record.
A cultural guide can therefore invite visitors to look in two directions at once — toward the stories and experiences that shaped earlier generations, and toward the people who continue to define Tsuut’ina identity today.
